meta.title: Design for How People Think: Using Brain Science to Build Better Products
meta.author: John Whalen, PhD

parts.title: Introduction to Why Design and Psychology Matter

sentences: The preface introduces why the **author** wrote this book, emphasizing the application of **psychology** in **product design**.
Many people are surprised that a psychologist can contribute to this field, often asking if they're being analyzed.
The book provides a path for designing **great experiences** by combining various **cognitive processes** and **senses**.
It highlights that people aren't always aware of their own mental processes, like **recognizing colors** without conscious awareness.

The author, trained in **cognitive science**, shares insights to improve products, aiming to help **product managers** and designers identify these cognitive aspects and use **interviews** to enhance the design process, ensuring products meet the audience's needs effectively.
This hands-on, practical guide is meant for professionals eager to create exceptional, memorable experiences.
The **Six Minds framework** outlined aims to better understand and segment audience needs for successful product development.

parts.title: Preface: Engaging Psychologists and Cognitive Scientists

sentences: In a **practical** book, the author can't cover all the **nuances** of the mind/brain but aims to communicate relevant information on designing products and services with an understanding of cognitive processes.
The goal is to have a **psychologically driven design** process and integrate what we know about our **minds** into product design.
The author encourages feedback from psychologists and cognitive scientists to refine his approach.
**Memory** and **perception** often work in **abstract** ways rather than detailed ones.
People use **stereotypes**, conceptual **memories**, and **mental models** to quickly process visual scenes and interactions.

For example, when asked to distinguish a US penny from similar images, most people struggle because their memory doesn't store all the specific details of the coin; it stores a general **concept** of it.
The phenomenon of **boundary extension** occurs when the mind fills in gaps beyond the **edges** of a scene based on **assumptions**.

This cognitive tendency can be applied positively in **product** and **service design** by creating experiences that align with users' **stereotypes** and expectations—leading to a more intuitive and trustworthy interaction without needing thorough instructions or explanations.

parts.title: Language and Semantic Design in Communication

sentences: We focus on **language and semantics** in design.
Language helps us understand how **audiences** perceive our products.
But words can have different meanings for different people.
**Laypeople** and **experts** might use different terms, like in **healthcare** jargon.
This impacts product **trust** and **experience**.
Communication can fail when overusing **jargon** or misaligning with consumer **understanding**.
This applies to **texting** habits, where terms vary by culture or age.
Designers should ensure people feel like 'you're speaking my language' to create comfort.
Notably, **translations** can alter meanings in different regions, like a **Chesterfield** in Canada is a **couch** in the US.
Interviews help identify the exact terms clients use, bridging the experience divide.

parts.title: Unlocking User Needs Through Contextual Interviews

sentences: **Contextual interviews** combine **watching** and **interviewing** people in their **natural settings** to uncover the "**why**" behind their behaviors.

Unlike traditional focus groups and surveys, contextual interviews help reveal **unconscious actions** and **nuances** in customer behavior, allowing for a deep understanding needed for **successful product design**.
By observing **superusers** and the environments where users live, researchers can gather critical insights into **inefficiencies** and **innovations** that are often overlooked.
This hands-on approach helps in **stepping into users' minds**, adapting a customer-centric perspective, and uncovering **hidden opportunities** to enhance user experiences.

**Wayfinding** involves understanding where users think they are in virtual or **physical space**, how they expect to navigate from **Point A** to **Point B**, and the **cues** they use to determine their location.
In product design, it is crucial to incorporate virtual **signposts** or cues to help users orient themselves and know their path within a system.
Understanding users’ expectations and how they fill in gaps in their navigation is vital.
In terms of **navigation strategies**, users may rely on external tools like **search engines** for assistance.
When designing **products or services**, it is important to consider the entire ecosystem and **non-obvious** pathways users might take based on their past experiences or **assumptions**.
Observing users can reveal unexpected **workarounds** and "tricks" they use, which help in tailoring better **interaction designs** that meet user needs and expectations.

parts.title: Exploring User Emotion in Product Design

sentences: **Emotion** is one of the six key factors influencing how users interact with products.

It suggests considering emotions on three levels: **Appeal** (what instantly attracts customers), **Enhance** (factors that add meaningful value over time), and **Awaken** (elements that align with users’ deeper aspirations and fears).
Understanding these dimensions helps design products that cater to immediate reactions as well as long-term desires and anxieties.
This approach uses insights from **Daniel Kahneman** about loss and gain, emphasizing the importance of understanding **users' fears** alongside their goals.
The content discusses **emotional impact on financial decisions** and **user interface design**.
Customers reacted emotionally to credit-related issues like identity theft, displaying **fear** and **anxiety**.
This influenced their decision-making, showing the powerful role of emotions in consumer behavior.
Designers must address these emotions to restore trust and improve experiences.
In user interface design, the **Six Minds framework** helps understand user behavior and design better.
It involves aspects like **language**, **emotion**, and **wayfinding**.
By analyzing these, designers can identify **user segments** to create tailored product experiences, enhancing usability and satisfaction.

parts.title: Using the Six Minds in the Double Diamond Process

sentences: The **Double Diamond** design process includes: **Discover, Define, Develop, and Deliver**.
Using the **Six Minds** method helps to efficiently empathize with user needs during the discovery and definition stages.
The aim is to identify opportunities to appeal, enhance, and awaken audience passions, thus refining problem-solving before pursuing design solutions.

In the second diamond (develop and deliver), **vision/attention**, **wayfinding**, **memory**, and **problem solving** are key to informing and constraining design choices by understanding how users interact with products.
You're equipped to **design experiences** using the "Six Minds" framework, resulting in **better, faster design outcomes** with less debate.
This chapter summarizes the journey so far and previews possible **outcomes from employing the Six Minds**.

Unique to this approach is the inclusion of **empathy at various cognitive levels**—acknowledging not just the user’s functional problems but also considering cognitive systems like **language, decision-making**, and **emotional qualities** during design.
Every “experience” entails numerous “**micro-experiences**” that collectively shape the perception of a singular event, like the series of experiences during an airport visit.
Recognizing that experiences are often **a series of interconnected moments** prompts us to consider the **cumulative impact** while designing.
